openings.name: Scotch Game

notes.9: 4...g5 is the sharpest Budapest idea - kick the bishop and hold the kingside.
4.Nf3 heads for the h6 and g4 squares and challenges Black for the g4 outpost.

notes.1: 1.d4 claims the centre and heads for the c4 outpost.
notes.2: ...Nf6 attacks e4 and keeps White out of d5.
notes.3: 2.c4 strikes at the d5 pawn and offers to open the centre.
notes.4: ...e5! refuses the gambit and attacks the d4 pawn instead.
notes.5: 3.dxe5 accepts the challenge and attacks ...Ng4.
notes.6: ...Ng4! retreats with tempo, setting up a long pin against the queen.
notes.7: 3.Bf4! pins the g8 knight and prevents ...Nh6 winning the e5 pawn.

keyIdeas: Black's plan is always ...Nh6, ...Be7, ...f6 and ...c6 to keep the bind.
The queen's knight often ends up on f6 for a long-term e5 blockade.
For White: Ne2, Bg3, Bd3 and Qc2 to relieve the pin and play f4.
The e5 pawn is Black's headache — it wants to reach e4 and expand.
traps: Without 3.Bf4, ...Nh6 can simply win the e5 pawn.
Over-eager f4 advances can be met by ...c5 and a strong counterattack on the d4 pawn.

openings.name: Scandinavian Defence
openings.description: Black attacks e4 immediately and heads for an early queen swap. Simple, tough, and a great way to learn how to defend before you know any theory.

notes.7: 3...Qa5 stops an early e5 push and eyes c3 and b2 - the queen's second sortie.
4.d4 builds the ideal pawn centre and punishes the queen's trip away from home.

notes.8: 4...Bf5 develops the c8-bishop with tempo, attacking e2 and the king.

notes.1: 1.e4 takes the centre and eyes e5 and d5.
notes.2: ...d5! challenges e4 head-on and opens lines toward the white king.
notes.3: 2.exd5 accepts the challenge and opens the e-file and d-file.
notes.4: ...Qxd5! hits e4 with tempo and simplifies the position early.
notes.5: 3.Nc3 develops and attacks the d5 queen.
notes.6: ...Qa5! steps aside with tempo, keeping the c3 knight tied down.

keyIdeas: Trade into a simple position where your bishops and pawns do the work.
For Black: Nf6, Be7, O-O and e6 build a solid wall.
For White: Be2, O-O and Nf3 develop normally — you have the easier game.
The early queen swap often favours White slightly, so play solidly afterwards.
traps: After ...Qa5, 4.d4 leads to the Modern Scandinavian; the main line is 4.Nf3 Bf5.
Grabbing on c3 without support loses a pawn — Black usually can't afford doubled pawns.

openings.name: Vienna Game
openings.description: Black plays ...e5, ...Nc6 and then moves the f8 bishop to c5 — a small extra tempo that leads to genuinely strategic middlegames from move three.

notes.7: 3.f4 is the Vienna Gambit - pawn after pawn, aiming at a quick attack.

notes.9: 3...Nf6 4.d4 transposes into the Scotch and Two Knights, where White has the better count.

notes.7: 3...Bc5 develops the bishop early with tempo, which is the whole Vienna idea.

notes.1: 1.e4 takes the centre and eyes e5 and d5.
notes.2: ...e5! takes the centre and challenges White's e4 pawn head-on.
notes.3: 2.Nc3 develops with tempo, defending e4 and attacking the d5/e5 squares.
notes.4: ...Nc6! defends e5 and attacks the d4 square.
notes.5: 3.Bc4 develops toward f7 and prepares the d2-d4 break.
notes.6: ...Bc5! the Vienna move — developing the bishop before castling and seizing a tempo.

keyIdeas: The ...Bc5 tempo is worth real points; use it to prepare a quick f7 attack.
For White: d3 first (the Frankenstein-Dracula) leads to excellent piece play.
Nge2, d4 and O-O build a solid position with good piece coordination.
Transpose to the Italian or the Scotch if Black takes the bishop back.
traps: Playing d4 too early lets Black build a strong e5 centre and free the c8 bishop.
3.Nf3 lets Black play ...d6 and keep the bishop free for a6-b5 ideas.

openings.name: Polish Defence (Centre Game)
openings.description: Black takes the centre with ...d5, trades into a knights-versus-bishops endgame and hopes to reach a simplified, favourable pawn endgame.

notes.11: 5...Nd7 retreats the knight to defend d5 - Black trades a pawn for a durable position.

notes.9: 4...dxe4 takes the e4 pawn at once, relying on activity over structure.

notes.11: 5...Nd7 6.Nxe5 wins a pawn back and attacks the c6 knight.

notes.1: 1.e4 takes the centre and eyes e5 and d5.
notes.2: ...e5! takes the centre and challenges White’s e4 pawn head-on.
notes.3: 2.d4 builds the biggest centre in chess.
notes.4: ...d5! meets the challenge — the Polish Defence’s core idea.
notes.5: 3.Nc3 develops and attacks the e4 and d5 squares.
notes.6: ...Nf6! develops with tempo, challenging the e4 pawn a second time.
notes.7: 4.Nf3 defends e4 and adds another attacker — Black still wants to simplify.
notes.8: 4...Nxe4! grabs a pawn and heads for a simplifying trade.
notes.9: 5.Nxe4! recaptures — most players take, keeping the initiative for White.
notes.10: 5...Nd7 develops the knight, avoiding doubled pawns and aiming for an endgame advantage.

keyIdeas: Black plans to trade pieces and reach a favourable bishops-vs-knights endgame.
Refusing ...Nxe4 with dxe4 leads to the pawn endgame (the Polish Gambit).
The b2 bishop is Black's best piece in the resulting structures.
For White: keep the position complex and push the c-pawn for counterplay.
traps: Taking on e4 with the pawn (4.dxe4) is a gambit that backfires if Black centralises quickly.
Missing the recapture 4.Nxe4 leaves a knight on e4 with no support — usually bad.

openings.name: French Defence — Classical (Steinitz)
openings.description: The quiet answer to 1.e4: Black builds a rock-solid d5/e5 wall, keeps the c8 bishop for the endgame and attacks White's e4 pawn piece by piece.

notes.9: 4...Be7 declines the pin and saves the c8-bishop for the endgame.
5...c5 immediately strikes the pawn chain White has just built.

notes.7: 3.c4 is the Macutari gambit: White offers the c-pawn to wreck the d5 centre.

notes.1: 1.e4 takes the centre and eyes e5 and d5.
notes.2: ...e6! challenges e4 from the side and prepares ...d5.
notes.3: 2.d4 builds the biggest centre in chess.
notes.4: ...d5! meets the challenge and claims the centre for Black.
notes.5: 3.Nc3 develops and attacks the e4 and d5 squares.
notes.6: ...Nf6 develops twice and eyes the e4 pawn.
notes.7: 3.Bg5 pins the f6 knight, which often ends up defending e4.
notes.8: ...Be7 develops and keeps the dark-squared bishop free for the endgame.
notes.9: 4.e5! kicks the knight away and locks in the classic French structure.
notes.10: ...Nfd7! retreats calmly to the ideal blockading square — the Steinitz defence.

keyIdeas: Blockade on d6 and c6 and attack the e4 pawn piece by piece.
Trade into an endgame where the e5 and c5 pawns are easy to attack.
Be7 and Nfd7 form the classic Steinitz set-up.
For White: keep the e4 pawn healthy with d3/d4 and avoid early queenside play.
traps: 4.e5 without f4 or d3 support can be met by ...c5 and ...f6, winning the e5 pawn.
O-O-O without ...b6 and ...Bb7 can be met by Ba6, hitting the c4 pawn.
